          CE STEPHENS PROPERTIES, LLC’S POST HEARING INITIAL BRIEF

         CE Stephens Properties, LLC (CE Stephens or Party 642) hereby files its Post Hearing

Initial Brief, and respectfully urges Your Honors to recommend that the Commission approve the

Applicants’ proposed Route 894, and in support thereof shows as follows:

I.       INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY

         At the outset, CE Stephens expresses its sincere thanks for the Administrative Law Judges’

(ALJs) attention to this case, their attention to the parties’ arguments and testimonies, and the

ALJs’ patience with the parties in this proceeding.

         It is the parties’ task in this proceeding to assist the ALJs and the Commissioners in

selecting a route for the Applicants’ 1 proposed Bell County East to Big Hill transmission line

guided by the Public Utility Regulatory Act 2 and the Public Utility Commission of Texas’s




1
     Oncor Electric Delivery Company and Lower Colorado River Authority TSC (Oncor, or LCRA TSC,
     respectively, or collectively the Applicants).
2

 (Commission) Substantive Rules. 3 Paramount in carrying out that task are the routing criteria the

Commission adopted for selecting a path for a new transmission line.

        Crucially, a landowner not wanting the line on or near their property is not a differentiating

factor in selecting a route for the line. Precisely because of that common thread amongst the

landowners, the Commission adopted the routing criteria shown in its CCN Application form, and

that over the years through its orders, has refined.

        Similarly, during the Hearing, Your Honors heard many instances of intervenors asking

the Applicants’ witness panel on cross-examination whether the existence of an anecdotal fact—

or the mere fact that the line would run across their property—would help either inform or change

the Applicants’, and ultimately the Commission’s, selection of which route best meets the factors

set forth in 16 TAC 25.101. CE Stephens urges Your Honors to find that the discussion of

anecdotal facts singularly pertaining to the detrimental impact a line would have on a landowner’s

property; a habitable structure not identified in the Environmental Assessment (EA); or any other

anecdotal piece of data that is not substantiated by authenticated record evidence should be

afforded no weight by Your Honors.

        Most parties, including the Applicants, look to the Commission’s routing criteria and

invariably point to a route or routes they believe “best meets” those criteria. And the Applicants

did no differently in this proceeding identifying Alternative Route No. 894 (Route 894) as the

route out of 122 potential filed routes that best meets the Commission’s routing criteria, that is, the

“Best Meets” route.

          Though identifying a best-meets route, the Applicants nonetheless are heard to stress that

all 122 routes they show on their maps will meet the Commission’s routing criteria 4 – and this is

not surprising given that their bottom-line goal is to build a transmission line from Point A to Point

B.    While perhaps not wholly indifferent to cost or impacts of the Applicants’ proposed

transmission line on landowners or their land, if the Commission selected the longest, most

expensive line traversing land never spoiled by a transmission line before, traveling over pristine

territory, crossing multiple waterways and endangered-species habitat, and through the middle of

a town, the Applicants would undertake to build that line.                     But in selecting a route the

Commission’s decision is not based on blindly throwing darts at a target with the hopes of finding

the best solution under the circumstances, i.e., that virtually no landowner wants the line on or near

their property.

         Instead, the Commission’s decision is informed by its routing criteria, 5 involving a review

undertaken not on a link-by-link basis, but instead an assessment performed on how a route – end

to end – best meets the Commission’s routing criteria. And notwithstanding the Applicants’

position that any of the 122 filed routes will satisfy the Commission’s routing criteria, the

Applicants nonetheless identify a route that best meets the Commission’s routing criteria. Here,

the Applicants identified Route 894 as the “Best Meets” route.

         After review of the Applicants’ Application, their witnesses’ testimonies, and in particular

their Environmental Assessment (EA), Ms. Christine Magers, CE Stephens’ expert witness in this

proceeding, concluded that: (1) routes that use Links N4 perform poorly compared to Route 894. 6

more specifically, the Applicants identified Route 894 as the best meets route because:

                  1.       Link N4 Would Result in Fragmentation

         Link N4 would bisect CE Stephens’ property, Sola Fe Ranch, across the middle of the

property from east to west. 13          As Ms. Magers testified, “the proposed transmission line

construction and operation will result in substantial, devastating, long-term impacts to [Sola Fe

Ranch], natural resources, and other human resources along the ROW and associated access roads,

substations, and infrastructure.” 14 Moreover, based on the approximately 3,800-foot length of Link

N4 across the Stephens Property, the ROW alone would directly affect approximately 17 acres,

before accounting for additional disturbances associated with access roads, structure work areas,

construction staging, grading, and other temporary and permanent workspaces.” 15

         Crucially, the impacts of any route that uses Link N4 would extend beyond the acreage

physically occupied by the ROW. As Ms. Magers explained, the Link N4 ROW corridor would

divide Sola Fe Ranch in half, fragment habitat, affect wildlife movement, alter visual character,

create new access and maintenance burdens, and significantly negatively impact the owner’s use

of the property. 16

482, and a separate parcel of land not identified on Oncor/LCRA’s map. 17 The fragmentation Link

brushland, grassland, rocky upland, drainage, and water-associated habitat. 25 Those habitats

                   2.      Link N4 Would Detrimentally Impact Land Use Along N4

         Routes using Link N4 will affect existing land use along Link N4 and Sola Fe Ranch. 35

The existing land use along Link N4 is inextricably intertwined with ranching, hunting, wildlife

habitat, and watershed protection.

         The Stephens’ Sola Fe Ranch is used for exotic wildlife management, hunting, and outdoor

recreation. 36 Sola Fe Ranch depends on coordinated land management, controlled access, habitat

quality, fencing, water infrastructure, ranch roads, wildlife movement, security, and the ability to

manage the Property as an integrated business operation. 37 Any Alternative Route utilizing Link

N4 would deprive not just the Stephens of their lands intended use, but also the hunting and outdoor

community that the Property serves as a source of outdoor recreation.

         As the owner of Sola Fe Ranch, Ms. Erin Stephens, testified, Sola Fe Ranch has Sable,

Bongo, Kudu, Roan, Impala, Blackbuck, Fallow, Grants Gazelle, Addax, and Scimitar Horned

Oryx on the Property. 38 Ms. Magers also testified that, during her visit to the Property, she

personally observed sable antelope, impala, bongo antelope, roan antelope, dama gazelle, and

scimitar-horned oryx. 39 Crucially, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN)

Red List of Threatened Species lists the bongo as near threatened, the dama gazelle as critically

endangered, and the scimitar-horned oryx as endangered. 40 The use of any route using Link N4

would detrimentally affect the exotic, near threatened, and endangered species on Sola Fe Ranch.

maintaining agricultural production goals. 42             The existence of these conservation-oriented

recognized habitat and watershed value by the state.

         CE Stephens acknowledges that the ALJs are not to analyze a link in isolation; however, it

is important to point out that every route (including Routes 487, 572, and CCG) that uses Link N4

Accordingly, not only will routes that use Link N4 impact at least eleven more habitable structures,

land on Link N4 for hunting, outdoor recreation, and conservation of exotic wildlife.

         Therefore, CE Stephens urges Your Honors to reject any recommended route that uses

Link N4.
